# Toy of the Year 1997

## Eh-oh! It's the Teletubbies!

**Tinky Winky, Dipsy, La-la and Po have swept aside all competitors to win the top award in the UK toy industry, the British Association of Toy Retailer’s (BATR) Toy of the Year 1997/1998.**

The award was presented in front of an audience of around 600 from both sides of the toy industry at a gala dinner at the Royal Lancaster Hotel, London on Sunday 1st February 1998.

BATR chairman, David Fogel says, “In an industry dominated by powerful multi-national companies, I am delighted that our award has been won by a family-run British toy company, Golden Bear in Telford, with toys based on a British television programme.”

The originators of the ‘virtual pets’ craze raging around the world, Tamagotchi (Bandai) won most Innovative Toy of the Year, Hasbro’s Action Man Skydiver was Boy’s Toy of the Year, while a Spanish company, Famosa scooped Girl’s Toy of the Year with a doll that can change it’s expression. Star Wars Monopoly (Waddingtons) was voted Game of the Year.

Toy Options, with Buzz Lightyear in 1996 (which continued high sales right through 1997) and Spice Girls dolls which only arrived in December, won Toy Company of the Year award.

## THE BATR TOY AWARDS 1997/98

| Award | Winner | Other Nominations |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |
| **BATR Toy of the Year** | **Teletubbies (Golden Bear)** |  |
| Most Innovative Toy | Tamagotchi (Bandai) | Nano Pals (Playmates) Barcode Truck (Lego) |
| Game of the Year | Star Wars Monopoly (Waddingtons) | Jenga (MB Games) Goosebumps (Waddingtons) |
| Boys Toy of the Year | Action Man Skydiver (Hasbro) | Buzz Lightyear (Toy Options) Micro Machines (Hasbro) |
| Girls Toy of the Year | Baby Expressions (Famosa) | Pet Doctor Barbie (Mattel) Magic Moving Polly Pocket (Bluebird) |
| Pre-School Toy of the Year | Tickle Me Elmo (Tyco) | Thomas the Tank Engine (Ertl) Pooh Bear range (Mattel) |
| Activity Toy of the Year | Get Set Chocolate Factory (Waddingtons) |  |
| Toy Company of the Year | Toy Options Limited Suppliers of Buzz Lightyear and Spice Girls Dolls |  |

## Notes for Editors

The BATR represents over 75% of the UK toy trade with members including Toys R Us, Woolworths, Index, Hamleys, Early Learning, Safeway, Tesco as well as all the members of the Toymaster and Youngsters groups.

**Waddingtons** was a British manufacturer of [card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Card_games "Card games") and [board games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_games "Board games"). The company was founded by John Waddington of [Leeds, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds,_England "Leeds, England") and the manager, actor and playwright [Wilson Barrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Barrett "Wilson Barrett"), under the name _Waddingtons Limited_. The name was changed in 1905 to _John Waddington Limited_, then _Waddington's House of Games_, then _Waddington Games_, and finally just _Waddingtons_.

## Founding and history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Waddingtons&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Founding and history")]

The company was established as a printing business, and at first 'practically all its business related to the theatre'.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-1) It entered into game production in 1922, due to a boom in demand for playing cards around [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-TTT-2) Waddingtons subsequently sold both original games (especially tie-ins for UK television programmes) and games licensed from other publishers.

Waddingtons became the UK publisher of the US [Parker Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parker_Brothers "Parker Brothers")' [Monopoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopoly_(game) "Monopoly (game)"), while Parker licensed Waddingtons' [Cluedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluedo "Cluedo").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-TTT-2) In 1941, the British [Directorate of Military Intelligence section 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MI9 "MI9") (MI9) had the company create a special edition of Monopoly for [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II")[prisoners of war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war "Prisoner of war") held by the Germans.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-3) Hidden inside these games were maps, compasses, real money and other objects useful for escaping. They were distributed to prisoners by fake charitable organisations.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-4) In 2024, an immersive, life-sized monopoly was created in Leeds in honor of Waddingtons.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-5)

In the years 1971 to 1985 the firm printed 13 different sets of postage stamps for the Hong Kong Post Office.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-6)

[Victor Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Watson "Victor Watson"), the grandson of Victor Hugo Watson was its chairman from 1977 to 1993.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-8) While well known for games, they never provided more than 15% of profit; Victor continued his father Norman's emphasis on improving packaging technology, such as folding cartons and microwave trays. From the 1970s, the popularity of [video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game "Video game") hurt game sales, and after Victor's retirement,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-9) the company was bought by [Hasbro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasbro "Hasbro") in 1994.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-10)

Beginning in 1994, [Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas "Christmas")-themed [jigsaw puzzles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jigsaw_puzzles "Jigsaw puzzles") were released annually until 2007. The first twelve in the series depicted a scene from a [Victorian-era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era "Victorian era") Christmas. The final puzzle depicted a scene from the [fairy tale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairy_tale "Fairy tale")[Cinderella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinderella "Cinderella"). The small number of puzzles, combined with them being limited editions, has made these puzzles highly collectable. Further jigsaws have been produced since 2010 by a new company, using the same brand name.

**Waddingtons** was a British manufacturer of [card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Card_games "Card games") and [board games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_games "Board games"). The company was founded by John Waddington of [Leeds, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds,_England "Leeds, England") and the manager, actor and playwright [Wilson Barrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Barrett "Wilson Barrett"), under the name _Waddingtons Limited_. The name was changed in 1905 to _John Waddington Limited_, then _Waddington's House of Games_, then _Waddington Games_, and finally just _Waddingtons_.

## Founding and history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Waddingtons&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Founding and history")]

The company was established as a printing business, and at first 'practically all its business related to the theatre'.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-1) It entered into game production in 1922, due to a boom in demand for playing cards around [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-TTT-2) Waddingtons subsequently sold both original games (especially tie-ins for UK television programmes) and games licensed from other publishers.

Waddingtons became the UK publisher of the US [Parker Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parker_Brothers "Parker Brothers")' [Monopoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopoly_(game) "Monopoly (game)"), while Parker licensed Waddingtons' [Cluedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluedo "Cluedo").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-TTT-2) In 1941, the British [Directorate of Military Intelligence section 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MI9 "MI9") (MI9) had the company create a special edition of Monopoly for [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II")[prisoners of war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war "Prisoner of war") held by the Germans.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-3) Hidden inside these games were maps, compasses, real money and other objects useful for escaping. They were distributed to prisoners by fake charitable organisations.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-4) In 2024, an immersive, life-sized monopoly was created in Leeds in honor of Waddingtons.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-5)

In the years 1971 to 1985 the firm printed 13 different sets of postage stamps for the Hong Kong Post Office.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-6)

[Victor Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Watson "Victor Watson"), the grandson of Victor Hugo Watson was its chairman from 1977 to 1993.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-8) While well known for games, they never provided more than 15% of profit; Victor continued his father Norman's emphasis on improving packaging technology, such as folding cartons and microwave trays. From the 1970s, the popularity of [video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game "Video game") hurt game sales, and after Victor's retirement,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-9) the company was bought by [Hasbro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasbro "Hasbro") in 1994.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waddingtons#cite_note-10)

Beginning in 1994, [Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas "Christmas")-themed [jigsaw puzzles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jigsaw_puzzles "Jigsaw puzzles") were released annually until 2007. The first twelve in the series depicted a scene from a [Victorian-era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era "Victorian era") Christmas. The final puzzle depicted a scene from the [fairy tale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairy_tale "Fairy tale")[Cinderella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinderella "Cinderella"). The small number of puzzles, combined with them being limited editions, has made these puzzles highly collectable. Further jigsaws have been produced since 2010 by a new company, using the same brand name.

**Tyco Toys** was an American toy manufacturer. It was acquired by [Mattel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattel "Mattel") in 1997,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-nyt_mattel_1996-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-nyt_mattel_1997-2) becoming one of its brands.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tyco_Toys&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Formation of Tyco

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tyco_Toys&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Formation of Tyco")]

The company was established as Mantua Metal Products by John Tyler and Jim Thomas in 1926, producing model boats and electric motors to power them out of [Mantua, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantua_Township,_New_Jersey "Mantua Township, New Jersey"). They began to produce motors for train models of all sizes. Then, in 1933, the business was moved to [Woodbury Heights, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodbury_Heights,_New_Jersey "Woodbury Heights, New Jersey"). By 1937, Mantua began selling its own ready-to-run [HO scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HO_scale "HO scale")[model train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_modelling "Rail transport modelling").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:2-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4)

From 1942 to 1945, the production of model railroad products was suspended as the company participated in the manufacturing of precision measuring and mapping equipment for the U.S. Army and Navy in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). The company received the [Army-Navy "E" Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army-Navy_%22E%22_Award "Army-Navy \"E\" Award") for excellence in production in 1945. After the war, they converted the plant back to the production of model railroading equipment. Thomas left the company in 1947 to start his own train line. Mantua began using plastic in its trains starting in the 1950s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4)

Tyler Manufacturing Company was formed in 1953 by Tyler and marketing director Milt Grey to focus on ready-to-run trains for younger children.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:42-5) This new effort brought them into the toy business, where their offerings were sold at discount stores and toy stores in addition to hobby shops. Tyler's smaller trains also meant they could fit more on a shelf than competitors like [Lionel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Corporation "Lionel Corporation") and [Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Marx_and_Company "Louis Marx and Company"). A wide range of slot cars and repair parts, track sections, controllers and accessories were also available.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-Train_Collectors_Society2-6) By 1957, the company had a roster of 11 locomotives. That year, Tyco became an official nameplate for its line of ready-to-run trains. In 1963, it also began selling HO scale electric racing, or 'slot car' sets.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-7)

In 1967, Mantua and Tyler Manufacturing Company were merged to create Tyco Industries. John Tyler's son Norman Tyler was named president of the combined entity.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:42-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:13-8) By the 1970s, Tyco shifted sales and marketing to a consumer-oriented, mass marketing focus.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4)

### Corporate ownership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tyco_Toys&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Corporate ownership")]

In 1970, the company was sold to [Consolidated Foods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Lee_Corporation "Sara Lee Corporation").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-Train_Collectors_Society2-6) Manufacturing was moved from New Jersey to Hong Kong and new, more fantastical trains were produced during this time. By 1972, the Mantua name was replaced by Tyco Industries, and the company moved to [Mount Laurel, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Laurel,_New_Jersey "Mount Laurel, New Jersey"). Tyco had become unprofitable and new leadership was brought in, including Richard Grey as president.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:4-9)

During the 1970s the train model market lost much of its former allure and Tyco's sales suffered due to the popularity of electronic toys. In order to withstand the public's dwindling interest in trains, the company began to diversify.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:4-9) In 1977, Norman Tyler, the son of Tyco's founder, bought the original factory and split off Mantua as a separate company.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:2-3)

In 1981, Consolidated sold Tyco to Savoy Industries, an investment group led by Benson Seltzer, for $18.6 million.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:42-5)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:5-10) While Grey maintained that the firm's future was in toys, Seltzer's goal was to turn it into a diversified conglomerate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:9-11) Hoping to replace trains with something more suitable for the times, Tyco introduced its [US-1 Trucking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US-1_Trucks "US-1 Trucks") line of electric trucks.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-13) It proved to be an immediate success, though interest soon waned.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:4-9) The 1982 Tyco Catalog was the last to start off with H0-scale trains, signifying the company's change in priorities.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-14) In 1983, the company introduced Cliff Hangers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:4-9)

In 1984, Tyco produced its own interlocking brick product, called Super Blocks. They were heavily marketed as compatible with [Lego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lego "Lego") and [Duplo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lego_Duplo "Lego Duplo"),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-17) since the basic Lego patent expired in 1978.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-18) Lego sued Tyco in an attempt to halt the production of its [Lego clone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lego_clone "Lego clone"). Though Tyco won the case in 1987, limits were placed on the marketing and production of Super Blocks.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-Washington_Post22-19)

### Public company

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tyco_Toys&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Public company")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Battery_operated_water_guns_Playtime_Tyco_Amron.jpg/250px-Battery_operated_water_guns_Playtime_Tyco_Amron.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battery_operated_water_guns_Playtime_Tyco_Amron.jpg)

Battery operated [water guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_guns "Water guns") Playtime Tyco Amron

On February 20, 1986, Tyco became a publicly traded company[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:4-9) and had $87.7 million in revenue that year.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:5-10)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:3-20)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:13-8) Tyco revamped its RC brand at this time, teaming with the Japanese company Taiyo to release radio controlled cars with more powerful motors and dynamic suspensions, capable of performing in rugged conditions. They started with five models in the 1986 catalog, including the Turbo Hopper,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-21) before filling a full 13 pages with RC cars in 1987. By 1988, 22 pages of the company's catalog were taken up by Tyco R/C toys.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-23)

In 1987, the company moved away from its trucking line and model train offerings, instead focusing on newer toys.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-24) It debuted Tyco Super Dough to compete with [Play-Doh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play-Doh "Play-Doh"). Kenner quickly sued, citing similarities in the two products, but ultimately lost the case.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-25) Tyco debuted its [Dino-Riders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dino-Riders "Dino-Riders") line of dinosaur-based action figures in 1988.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-26) A cartoon series was produced to help market the line.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-27)

In May 1989, the company purchased the View-Master Ideal Group, Inc., which brought the [View-Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/View-Master "View-Master") line of [stereoscopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereoscope "Stereoscope"), [Magna Doodle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_Doodle "Magna Doodle") magnetic drawing toys, and [Ideal Nursery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_Toy_Company "Ideal Toy Company") line of dolls to Tyco.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-28) The company finished out the year with $384 million in revenue.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-Press-29) Between 1989 and 1991, Tyco teamed with [Sega Toys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Fave "Sega Fave") to distribute Pocket Power, a line of pocket-sized toys. A line for girls, called Pocket Pretties, was also developed.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-32)

Tyco's musical toys of the late 1980s and early 1990s included the Tyco Hot Lixx and Tyco Hot Keyz, an electronic guitar[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-33) and [keytar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keytar "Keytar") respectively.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-34)

After taking the company public, Seltzer was named chairman and maintained control of the board by filling it with family members and loyalists. In the years that followed, the company's stock valuation fell and revenue was impacted by Benson's self-serving investments. He lent money to and made acquisitions from his own companies. In 1988, he used Tyco's money to purchase an underwear company in Puerto Rico in which his family had an interest. Shareholders filed a lawsuit. By 1990, the situation came to a head.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:3-20) Seltzer and his two sons ultimately left the company and sold their remaining stock in July 1991.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:9-11) The news made Tyco's market valuation increase by 11%.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-35) President and CEO Richard Grey was then also named chairman.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-36)

Starting in the early 1990s, the company expanded internationally with its Tyco International operating unit. It opened wholly owned subsidiaries in the United Kingdom, Spain, France, Germany, Italy, Austria, Switzerland, Mexico, Canada, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg, and Australia.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:7-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-38) In October 1990, it bought Stanley Cohen's Playtime Toys[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-39) and turned the business into its direct import subsidiary.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:10-40)

In May 1992, Tyco purchased the [Matchbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matchbox_(brand) "Matchbox (brand)") brand of scale model cars for $106 million. The acquisition helped the company expand in international markets, such as England and Germany.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:13-8)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-Press-29)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-41) Tyco also purchased the Illco Toy Company in June, bringing Illco's extensive line of toys based on the children's show _[Sesame Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame\_Street "Sesame Street")_ to Tyco. It then put a greater emphasis on licensing popular characters from other companies.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:9-11) Later that year, Tyco signed a 10-year licensing agreement with [Children's Television Workshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame_Workshop "Sesame Workshop")[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-42) and Illco became the Tyco Preschool subsidiary.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:10-40)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-43) The company consolidated its domestic packing and distribution operations near Portland, Oregon by closing its plant in [Moorestown, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorestown,_New_Jersey "Moorestown, New Jersey") at the end of the year.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-44) Tyco had sales of $769 million in 1992.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:7-37) In the mid-1990s, as a bigger toy company, company headquarters was moved to [Mount Laurel, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Laurel,_New_Jersey "Mount Laurel, New Jersey").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In the 1990s, the company also branched out with other toys such as airplanes. Its hit toy of 1990 was a set of small quintuplet dolls, called the Quints, developed by [Bernard Loomis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Loomis "Bernard Loomis"). With a growing stable of accessories, it had generated $20 million after 10 months on the market.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-45) It made a hit in 1991 with their _[Disney's Little Mermaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Little\_Mermaid\_(1989\_film) "The Little Mermaid (1989 film)")_ dolls that were released in conjunction with the movie.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-46) In 1993, Tyco became the first company to license [Looney Tunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looney_Tunes "Looney Tunes") characters from Warner Bros.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:9-11) It also created the Power Plug, a third-party accessory that added turbo features and [macros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macro_(computer_science) "Macro (computer science)") to a [Sega Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Genesis "Sega Genesis") or [Super Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Super Nintendo Entertainment System") game controller.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-48)

After 1993, Tyco exited the model train business.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4) Gary Baughman was brought in as president in October 1994 and restructured the company. Tyco moved away from television and movie-related toy lines, refocusing the company on its classic offerings. The firm raised $96 million in a stock offering to pay down $40 million of debt. However, Tyco remained a distant third behind Mattel and Hasbro, bringing in $709.1 million in 1995. International operations were also consolidated into one central office in Belgium with satellite offices throughout Europe. However, the firm's overseas activity never rose above 25% of total sales.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:8-49) By 1996, Tyco had suffered three years of losses totalling $135.5 million.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-50)

Tyco's _Sesame Street_ line increased dramatically in popularity in 1996, when the plush doll [Tickle Me Elmo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tickle_Me_Elmo "Tickle Me Elmo") became the most sought-after toy of the Christmas season.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-People-51) The toy was released that July, with the company expecting to sell around 400,000 units. By December, Tyco had its four factories in China scrambling to produce 1 million units before Christmas.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-52)

### Purchase by Mattel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tyco_Toys&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Purchase by Mattel")]

In November 1996, Mattel announced it would acquire Tyco.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:0-53) At the time, Tyco was the third-largest toy company in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), with $709 million in sale the previous year.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:0-53) The combined company allowed Mattel to pair its strong distribution network with Tyco's products. It also meant Mattel would control a 19% share of the $13 billion U.S. toy market.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:8-49) The $755 million deal was approved by the FTC in March 1997 and nearly 10% (2,700 jobs) of the companies' combined workforce was eliminated. Mattel took a charge of $275 million for restructuring associated with the acquisition.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-54)

Tyco's Sesame Street, Magna Doodle, and View-Master toys were moved under Mattel's Fisher-Price brand. Matchbox, Tyco Electric Racing, and Tyco Radio Control products were placed under the Wheels division, alongside the [Hot Wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Wheels "Hot Wheels") brand.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-55)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:9-11) In 2005, Tyco's Mount Laurel offices were closed and operations were transferred to Mattel's El Segundo, California headquarters.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4)

Mantua Industries continued operations until October 2001, when its model railroad business was acquired by Model Power. Several items, such as steam engines and freight cars, were sold under its Mantua Classics brand.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4) The Mantua brand name was then licensed to Model Rectifier Corporation in 2014 before being bought by Lionel Corporation in 2018.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-57)

On February 23, 2019, Terry Flynn announced that Tyco was now a registered trademark of his Harden Creek Slot Cars, LLC. Flynn also has the Life Like trademark for slot cars.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tyco_Toys&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

Tyco's Mutator R/C car played a central role in the 1997 holiday-family comedy movie, _[Home Alone 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home\_Alone\_3 "Home Alone 3")_, where it is used as a concealer by the villains in a failed attempt to smuggle a highly classified electronic device into North Korea.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-59)

The company's [Garfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garfield "Garfield") telephone from the 1980s[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-60) became an infamous symbol of pollution when, starting in the 1980s, hundreds of these phones began washing up on the shores of [Brittany, France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany_(administrative_region) "Brittany (administrative region)"). This continued for 30 years, and the cause remained a mystery, until activists were able to find the source of the phones in 2019. A shipping container had been lost at sea and settled into a cave, where Garfield phones escaped into the environment for three decades.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-64)

**Tyco Toys** was an American toy manufacturer. It was acquired by [Mattel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattel "Mattel") in 1997,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-nyt_mattel_1996-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-nyt_mattel_1997-2) becoming one of its brands.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tyco_Toys&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Formation of Tyco

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tyco_Toys&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Formation of Tyco")]

The company was established as Mantua Metal Products by John Tyler and Jim Thomas in 1926, producing model boats and electric motors to power them out of [Mantua, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantua_Township,_New_Jersey "Mantua Township, New Jersey"). They began to produce motors for train models of all sizes. Then, in 1933, the business was moved to [Woodbury Heights, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodbury_Heights,_New_Jersey "Woodbury Heights, New Jersey"). By 1937, Mantua began selling its own ready-to-run [HO scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HO_scale "HO scale")[model train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_modelling "Rail transport modelling").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:2-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4)

From 1942 to 1945, the production of model railroad products was suspended as the company participated in the manufacturing of precision measuring and mapping equipment for the U.S. Army and Navy in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). The company received the [Army-Navy "E" Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army-Navy_%22E%22_Award "Army-Navy \"E\" Award") for excellence in production in 1945. After the war, they converted the plant back to the production of model railroading equipment. Thomas left the company in 1947 to start his own train line. Mantua began using plastic in its trains starting in the 1950s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4)

Tyler Manufacturing Company was formed in 1953 by Tyler and marketing director Milt Grey to focus on ready-to-run trains for younger children.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:42-5) This new effort brought them into the toy business, where their offerings were sold at discount stores and toy stores in addition to hobby shops. Tyler's smaller trains also meant they could fit more on a shelf than competitors like [Lionel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Corporation "Lionel Corporation") and [Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Marx_and_Company "Louis Marx and Company"). A wide range of slot cars and repair parts, track sections, controllers and accessories were also available.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-Train_Collectors_Society2-6) By 1957, the company had a roster of 11 locomotives. That year, Tyco became an official nameplate for its line of ready-to-run trains. In 1963, it also began selling HO scale electric racing, or 'slot car' sets.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-7)

In 1967, Mantua and Tyler Manufacturing Company were merged to create Tyco Industries. John Tyler's son Norman Tyler was named president of the combined entity.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:42-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:13-8) By the 1970s, Tyco shifted sales and marketing to a consumer-oriented, mass marketing focus.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4)

### Corporate ownership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tyco_Toys&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Corporate ownership")]

In 1970, the company was sold to [Consolidated Foods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Lee_Corporation "Sara Lee Corporation").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-Train_Collectors_Society2-6) Manufacturing was moved from New Jersey to Hong Kong and new, more fantastical trains were produced during this time. By 1972, the Mantua name was replaced by Tyco Industries, and the company moved to [Mount Laurel, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Laurel,_New_Jersey "Mount Laurel, New Jersey"). Tyco had become unprofitable and new leadership was brought in, including Richard Grey as president.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:4-9)

During the 1970s the train model market lost much of its former allure and Tyco's sales suffered due to the popularity of electronic toys. In order to withstand the public's dwindling interest in trains, the company began to diversify.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:4-9) In 1977, Norman Tyler, the son of Tyco's founder, bought the original factory and split off Mantua as a separate company.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:2-3)

In 1981, Consolidated sold Tyco to Savoy Industries, an investment group led by Benson Seltzer, for $18.6 million.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:42-5)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:5-10) While Grey maintained that the firm's future was in toys, Seltzer's goal was to turn it into a diversified conglomerate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:9-11) Hoping to replace trains with something more suitable for the times, Tyco introduced its [US-1 Trucking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US-1_Trucks "US-1 Trucks") line of electric trucks.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-13) It proved to be an immediate success, though interest soon waned.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:4-9) The 1982 Tyco Catalog was the last to start off with H0-scale trains, signifying the company's change in priorities.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-14) In 1983, the company introduced Cliff Hangers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:4-9)

In 1984, Tyco produced its own interlocking brick product, called Super Blocks. They were heavily marketed as compatible with [Lego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lego "Lego") and [Duplo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lego_Duplo "Lego Duplo"),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-17) since the basic Lego patent expired in 1978.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-18) Lego sued Tyco in an attempt to halt the production of its [Lego clone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lego_clone "Lego clone"). Though Tyco won the case in 1987, limits were placed on the marketing and production of Super Blocks.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-Washington_Post22-19)

### Public company

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tyco_Toys&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Public company")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Battery_operated_water_guns_Playtime_Tyco_Amron.jpg/250px-Battery_operated_water_guns_Playtime_Tyco_Amron.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battery_operated_water_guns_Playtime_Tyco_Amron.jpg)

Battery operated [water guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_guns "Water guns") Playtime Tyco Amron

On February 20, 1986, Tyco became a publicly traded company[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:4-9) and had $87.7 million in revenue that year.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:5-10)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:3-20)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:13-8) Tyco revamped its RC brand at this time, teaming with the Japanese company Taiyo to release radio controlled cars with more powerful motors and dynamic suspensions, capable of performing in rugged conditions. They started with five models in the 1986 catalog, including the Turbo Hopper,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-21) before filling a full 13 pages with RC cars in 1987. By 1988, 22 pages of the company's catalog were taken up by Tyco R/C toys.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-23)

In 1987, the company moved away from its trucking line and model train offerings, instead focusing on newer toys.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-24) It debuted Tyco Super Dough to compete with [Play-Doh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play-Doh "Play-Doh"). Kenner quickly sued, citing similarities in the two products, but ultimately lost the case.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-25) Tyco debuted its [Dino-Riders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dino-Riders "Dino-Riders") line of dinosaur-based action figures in 1988.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-26) A cartoon series was produced to help market the line.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-27)

In May 1989, the company purchased the View-Master Ideal Group, Inc., which brought the [View-Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/View-Master "View-Master") line of [stereoscopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereoscope "Stereoscope"), [Magna Doodle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_Doodle "Magna Doodle") magnetic drawing toys, and [Ideal Nursery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_Toy_Company "Ideal Toy Company") line of dolls to Tyco.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-28) The company finished out the year with $384 million in revenue.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-Press-29) Between 1989 and 1991, Tyco teamed with [Sega Toys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Fave "Sega Fave") to distribute Pocket Power, a line of pocket-sized toys. A line for girls, called Pocket Pretties, was also developed.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-32)

Tyco's musical toys of the late 1980s and early 1990s included the Tyco Hot Lixx and Tyco Hot Keyz, an electronic guitar[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-33) and [keytar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keytar "Keytar") respectively.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-34)

After taking the company public, Seltzer was named chairman and maintained control of the board by filling it with family members and loyalists. In the years that followed, the company's stock valuation fell and revenue was impacted by Benson's self-serving investments. He lent money to and made acquisitions from his own companies. In 1988, he used Tyco's money to purchase an underwear company in Puerto Rico in which his family had an interest. Shareholders filed a lawsuit. By 1990, the situation came to a head.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:3-20) Seltzer and his two sons ultimately left the company and sold their remaining stock in July 1991.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:9-11) The news made Tyco's market valuation increase by 11%.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-35) President and CEO Richard Grey was then also named chairman.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-36)

Starting in the early 1990s, the company expanded internationally with its Tyco International operating unit. It opened wholly owned subsidiaries in the United Kingdom, Spain, France, Germany, Italy, Austria, Switzerland, Mexico, Canada, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg, and Australia.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:7-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-38) In October 1990, it bought Stanley Cohen's Playtime Toys[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-39) and turned the business into its direct import subsidiary.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:10-40)

In May 1992, Tyco purchased the [Matchbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matchbox_(brand) "Matchbox (brand)") brand of scale model cars for $106 million. The acquisition helped the company expand in international markets, such as England and Germany.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:13-8)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-Press-29)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-41) Tyco also purchased the Illco Toy Company in June, bringing Illco's extensive line of toys based on the children's show _[Sesame Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame\_Street "Sesame Street")_ to Tyco. It then put a greater emphasis on licensing popular characters from other companies.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:9-11) Later that year, Tyco signed a 10-year licensing agreement with [Children's Television Workshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame_Workshop "Sesame Workshop")[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-42) and Illco became the Tyco Preschool subsidiary.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:10-40)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-43) The company consolidated its domestic packing and distribution operations near Portland, Oregon by closing its plant in [Moorestown, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorestown,_New_Jersey "Moorestown, New Jersey") at the end of the year.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-44) Tyco had sales of $769 million in 1992.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:7-37) In the mid-1990s, as a bigger toy company, company headquarters was moved to [Mount Laurel, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Laurel,_New_Jersey "Mount Laurel, New Jersey").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In the 1990s, the company also branched out with other toys such as airplanes. Its hit toy of 1990 was a set of small quintuplet dolls, called the Quints, developed by [Bernard Loomis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Loomis "Bernard Loomis"). With a growing stable of accessories, it had generated $20 million after 10 months on the market.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-45) It made a hit in 1991 with their _[Disney's Little Mermaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Little\_Mermaid\_(1989\_film) "The Little Mermaid (1989 film)")_ dolls that were released in conjunction with the movie.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-46) In 1993, Tyco became the first company to license [Looney Tunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looney_Tunes "Looney Tunes") characters from Warner Bros.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:9-11) It also created the Power Plug, a third-party accessory that added turbo features and [macros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macro_(computer_science) "Macro (computer science)") to a [Sega Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Genesis "Sega Genesis") or [Super Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Super Nintendo Entertainment System") game controller.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-48)

After 1993, Tyco exited the model train business.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4) Gary Baughman was brought in as president in October 1994 and restructured the company. Tyco moved away from television and movie-related toy lines, refocusing the company on its classic offerings. The firm raised $96 million in a stock offering to pay down $40 million of debt. However, Tyco remained a distant third behind Mattel and Hasbro, bringing in $709.1 million in 1995. International operations were also consolidated into one central office in Belgium with satellite offices throughout Europe. However, the firm's overseas activity never rose above 25% of total sales.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:8-49) By 1996, Tyco had suffered three years of losses totalling $135.5 million.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-50)

Tyco's _Sesame Street_ line increased dramatically in popularity in 1996, when the plush doll [Tickle Me Elmo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tickle_Me_Elmo "Tickle Me Elmo") became the most sought-after toy of the Christmas season.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-People-51) The toy was released that July, with the company expecting to sell around 400,000 units. By December, Tyco had its four factories in China scrambling to produce 1 million units before Christmas.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-52)

### Purchase by Mattel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tyco_Toys&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Purchase by Mattel")]

In November 1996, Mattel announced it would acquire Tyco.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:0-53) At the time, Tyco was the third-largest toy company in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), with $709 million in sale the previous year.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:0-53) The combined company allowed Mattel to pair its strong distribution network with Tyco's products. It also meant Mattel would control a 19% share of the $13 billion U.S. toy market.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:8-49) The $755 million deal was approved by the FTC in March 1997 and nearly 10% (2,700 jobs) of the companies' combined workforce was eliminated. Mattel took a charge of $275 million for restructuring associated with the acquisition.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-54)

Tyco's Sesame Street, Magna Doodle, and View-Master toys were moved under Mattel's Fisher-Price brand. Matchbox, Tyco Electric Racing, and Tyco Radio Control products were placed under the Wheels division, alongside the [Hot Wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Wheels "Hot Wheels") brand.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-55)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:9-11) In 2005, Tyco's Mount Laurel offices were closed and operations were transferred to Mattel's El Segundo, California headquarters.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4)

Mantua Industries continued operations until October 2001, when its model railroad business was acquired by Model Power. Several items, such as steam engines and freight cars, were sold under its Mantua Classics brand.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-:62-4) The Mantua brand name was then licensed to Model Rectifier Corporation in 2014 before being bought by Lionel Corporation in 2018.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-57)

On February 23, 2019, Terry Flynn announced that Tyco was now a registered trademark of his Harden Creek Slot Cars, LLC. Flynn also has the Life Like trademark for slot cars.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tyco_Toys&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

Tyco's Mutator R/C car played a central role in the 1997 holiday-family comedy movie, _[Home Alone 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home\_Alone\_3 "Home Alone 3")_, where it is used as a concealer by the villains in a failed attempt to smuggle a highly classified electronic device into North Korea.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-59)

The company's [Garfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garfield "Garfield") telephone from the 1980s[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-60) became an infamous symbol of pollution when, starting in the 1980s, hundreds of these phones began washing up on the shores of [Brittany, France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany_(administrative_region) "Brittany (administrative region)"). This continued for 30 years, and the cause remained a mystery, until activists were able to find the source of the phones in 2019. A shipping container had been lost at sea and settled into a cave, where Garfield phones escaped into the environment for three decades.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyco_Toys#cite_note-64)

_**Teletubbies**_ is a British [children's television series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_television_series "Children's television series") created by [Anne Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Wood "Anne Wood") and [Andrew Davenport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Davenport "Andrew Davenport") for the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"). The programme focuses on four differently coloured characters known as the Teletubbies, named after the television screens on their bellies. Recognised throughout [popular culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_culture "Popular culture") for the uniquely shaped [antenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_antenna "Television antenna") protruding from the head of each character, the Teletubbies communicate mostly through gibberish and were designed to bear resemblance to toddlers.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-6)

The series rapidly became a commercial success in Britain and abroad. It won multiple [BAFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_of_Film_and_Television_Arts "British Academy of Film and Television Arts") awards and was nominated for two [Daytime Emmys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytime_Emmy_Award "Daytime Emmy Award") throughout its run.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-BBC_News_Entertainment:_Tubbies_toast_another_three_years-7)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-bafta-2002-8) A [single based on the show's theme song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies_say_%22Eh-oh!%22 "Teletubbies say \"Eh-oh!\"") reached number 1 in the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart") in December 1997 and remained in the Top 75 for 32 weeks, selling over a million copies.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Spilsbury2012-9) By October 2000, the franchise generated over £1 billion ($1.6 billion) in merchandise sales.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-10)

Though the original run ended in 2001,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-11)[_[verification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] a rebooted series was green-lit in 2014.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-The_Guardian-12)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-13) The reboot premiered on [CBeebies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBeebies "CBeebies") in the United Kingdom and on the [Nick Jr. Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Jr._Channel "Nick Jr. Channel") in the United States.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-14) The reboot ran for 120 episodes, with the last episode airing on the Nick Jr. Channel on 17 August 2018.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-15) In 2022, a new version of the show premiered on [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") for American audiences.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-:0-16)

## Plot

The programme takes place in a grassy, floral landscape populated by [rabbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabbit "Rabbit") with [bird calls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_calls "Bird calls") audible in the background. The main shelter of the four Teletubbies is an [earth house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_house "Earth house") known as the "Tubbytronic Superdome" implanted in the ground and accessed through a hole at the top or an especially large semicircular door at the dome's foot. The Teletubbies co-exist with a number of strange contraptions such as the Voice Trumpets and the group's [anthropomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropomorphism "Anthropomorphism") blue [vacuum cleaner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_cleaner "Vacuum cleaner") ("Noo-Noo"). The show's colourful psychedelic setting was designed specifically to appeal to the attention spans of infants and unlock different sections of the mind while also educating young children of transitions that can be expected in life.

An assortment of rituals is performed throughout the course of every episode, such as the playful interactions between the Teletubbies and the Voice Trumpets, mishaps caused by the Noo-Noo, the footage of children displayed on the screens on the Teletubbies' stomachs, and the magical event[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-17) that occurs once per episode. The event differs each time; it is often caused inexplicably and is frequently strange yet whimsical. Each episode is closed by the Voice Trumpets and the narrator. The disappointed, reluctant, but obedient Teletubbies bid farewell to the viewer as they go back to the Tubbytronic Superdome while the Sun Baby sets.

He is green and named after his antenna, which resembles a [dipstick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dipstick "Dipstick"). Dipsy is the most stubborn of the Teletubbies, and will occasionally refuse to go along with the others' group opinion. She is red and has an antenna shaped like a stick used for blowing [soap bubbles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soap_bubble "Soap bubble"). Po normally speaks in a soft voice and has been stated by the show's creators to be [Cantonese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese_people "Cantonese people");[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-16things-20) she sometimes speaks [the language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese "Cantonese"). ## Release

On 31 March 1997, the first episode of _Teletubbies_ aired on [BBC2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Two "BBC Two") on the [CBBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBBC "CBBC") programming block. It filled a time slot previously held by _[Playdays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playdays "Playdays")_. This schedule change initially received backlash from parents, but the show was not moved.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Tegna-25) The programme's unconventional format quickly received attention from the media, and it was attracting two million viewers per episode by August.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-26) In February 1998, _[The Sydney Morning Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sydney\_Morning\_Herald "The Sydney Morning Herald")_ noted that it had "reached cult status" in less than a year on the air.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-27)

## Production

The show was created by Anne Wood and Andrew Davenport after the BBC requested their pitch for a show aimed at preschoolers. Inspired by Davenport's interest in [astronauts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"), specifically [Apollo 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11 "Apollo 11") and the first [Moon landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon_landing "Moon landing"), as well as their concern about "how children were reacting to the increasingly technological environment of the late 1990s", the two put together a pitch which the BBC picked up.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Howwemade-46)

Finding a shooting location was a challenge, as they wanted to film the production outside but were unable to locate a place "with a suitable bowl-like dip". They ended up filming on a farm in [Wimpstone, Warwickshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wimpstone,_Warwickshire "Wimpstone, Warwickshire"),[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-ourwarwickshire-org-47) where they had previously shot _[Tots TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tots\_TV "Tots TV")_.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Howwemade-46) Due to problems with a previous television show shooting at the location, the shooting was protested by the locals, although they calmed down after being assured that "it was a low-key children's programme and no one would be aware of the filming".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Howwemade-46) After the show took off, though, its popularity caused the land to be overrun by the press. In 2013, due to the continued trespassing, its owner, Rosemary Harding, had the location filled with water and turned into a small pond: "People were jumping fences and crossing cattle fields. We're glad to see the back of it."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-48)

According to Davenport, the press was particularly interested in getting photos of the actors in their Teletubby costumes without their heads on. Eventually, the team took measures to secure their privacy, including blindfolding visitors coming to the set and creating a tent for the actors to change in private.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Howwemade-46)

The artist who originally drew the characters that would become the Teletubbies was the illustrator and caricaturist Jonathan Hills, who also designed digital images for television programmes including _[Poirot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agatha\_Christie's\_Poirot "Agatha Christie's Poirot")_.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-49)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-50) In 2022 a sample from a collection of original drawings were presented by Hills' widow Lucy on the BBC show _[Antiques Roadshow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiques\_Roadshow "Antiques Roadshow")_. The collection was valued, by expert [Mark Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Hill_(antiques_expert) "Mark Hill (antiques expert)"), at up to £80,000.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-51)

## Promotion

### Merchandising

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/The_Teletubbies_are_still_here_2011_%286592747791%29.jpg/250px-The_Teletubbies_are_still_here_2011_%286592747791%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Teletubbies_are_still_here_2011_(6592747791).jpg)

A kiddie ride featuring the _Teletubbies_ characters

[Golden Bear Toys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Bear_Toys "Golden Bear Toys") distributed the first line of _Teletubbies_ dolls shortly after the programme's debut.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-52) They were sold internationally, with talking toys available in multiple languages.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-53)[Hasbro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasbro "Hasbro") signed on to develop a new range of products in 1998.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-54) In 1999, [Microsoft UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft") released a set of interactive "ActiMates" toys based on the characters.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-55) The Rasta Imposta company introduced _Teletubbies_ costumes for children and adults in the same year.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Blythe2011-56) Two educational [video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game "Video game") featuring the characters were also released throughout the series' run.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-57)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-58)

_Teletubbies_ dolls were the top-selling Christmas toy in 1997.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-59)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Holland2004-60) Demand outstripped supply at most retailers, reportedly prompting many shops to ration them to one per customer.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-61) In some cases, shoppers camped outside stores overnight in hopes of purchasing _Teletubbies_ merchandise.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-62)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-63) Fights over the toys broke out among parents and collectors on occasion.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Company2012-64)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Brewer2013-65) Over one million dolls were sold in Britain by 25 December of that year, with Golden Bear representatives estimating that sales could have reached three million if supplies had been available.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-66) The plush toys were named "Toy of the Year" by the [British Association of Toy Retailers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Association_of_Toy_Retailers "British Association of Toy Retailers") in 1998.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-67)

Kids' meal tie-ins have been released at [fast-food restaurants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast-food_restaurant "Fast-food restaurant") throughout North America. In May 1999, [Burger King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burger_King "Burger King") distributed a set of six _Teletubbies_ plush toys.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-68) They also included [chicken nuggets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicken_nugget "Chicken nugget") shaped like the characters on their menu for a brief period of time.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-RubinRubin2008-69) Keychains modelled after the characters were available at [McDonald's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonald's "McDonald's") in April 2000.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-70) These promotions became controversial among adults who believed they were intended to attract toddlers to high-fat food.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Schor2014-71) Psychiatrist [Alvin Francis Poussaint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_Francis_Poussaint "Alvin Francis Poussaint") considered the deals "troubling".[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-72) He voiced his opinion on the matter publicly, but did not take action against the companies.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-73)

Two [kiddie rides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiddie_ride "Kiddie ride") featuring the characters were manufactured by Jolly Roger.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-74) They were available at some amusement parks and arcades, such as [Chuck E. Cheese's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_E._Cheese's "Chuck E. Cheese's") and [Fantasy Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_Island_(UK_amusement_park) "Fantasy Island (UK amusement park)").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-75)

Overseas _Teletubbies_ merchandise sales throughout the 1990s delivered €136 million in profits for the BBC.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-76) By the time of the programme's cancellation, _Teletubbies_ toys had generated over £200 million in revenue for co-creator Anne Wood alone.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-77) In 2005, Chris Hastings and Ben Jones of _[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_ called _Teletubbies_ "the most lucrative show in BBC television history."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-78)

In 2021, WildBrain, who owns the Teletubbies brand, launched a Teletubbies Pride Collection, with merchandise proceeds going towards efforts to expand LGBTQ images and inclusion in children's and family programming.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-79)

To commemorate the tenth anniversary of the premiere of _Teletubbies_, a series of events took place from March to April 2007.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-tenth_anniversary-80) The characters headlined an invitation-only event in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") on 21 March 2007. They were also interviewed on [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC")'s _[The Today Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Today\_(NBC\_program) "Today (NBC program)")_ in an episode that included the first televised appearance of the actors without their costumes. A partnership was formed with [Isaac Mizrahi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Mizrahi "Isaac Mizrahi") in which Mizrahi designed Teletubbies-inspired bags to be [auctioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auction "Auction") off to benefit charities. Following their show in New York, the Teletubbies went on their first live European tour, performing in London, [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), [Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bremen "Bremen"), [Darmstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darmstadt "Darmstadt"), [Halle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halle_(Saale) "Halle (Saale)"), [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"), [Köln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ln "Köln"), and [Hannover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannover "Hannover").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-82)

## Reception

### Critical reception

[Common Sense Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Sense_Media "Common Sense Media")'s Emily Ashby found that "while the show's examples of cooperative play, wonder, and simple joys are gentle and pleasing, the creatures can still be a little grating to parents watching along."[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-89) Caryn James of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ stated in her review that the episodes "offer a genuinely appealing combination: cute and slightly surreal."[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-90) Writing in _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_, critic [Ray Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Richmond "Ray Richmond") described the show as "plenty surrealistic, all right, and loaded with bizarre Peter Max-style imagery that perfectly matches the Stepford-like quartet of techno trolls" and "a little bit slow for anyone over the age of, say, 30 months," but noted that "It's sweet, it's innocent, it's wholesome."[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-91)

Upon the show's release, some critics feared that the characters' use of babbling in place of complete sentences would negatively affect young viewers' ability to communicate. The _[Daily Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Mirror "Daily Mirror")_ reported in 1997 that many parents objected to its "goo-goo style" and "said the show was a bad influence on their children."[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-92) Marina Krcmar, a professor of communication at the [Wake Forest University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Forest_University "Wake Forest University"), told interviewers in 2007 that "toddlers learn more from an adult speaker than they do from a program such as _Teletubbies_."[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-93) However, Paul McCann of _[The Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Independent "The Independent")_ defended this aspect of the show, stating that "_Teletubbies_ upsets those who automatically assume that progressive and creative learning is trendy nonsense. Those who believe that education should be strictly disciplined and functional, even when you're 18 months old. Thankfully _Teletubbies_ isn't for them. It's for kids."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Tegna-25)

The programme's magical event that features a cut-out [lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lion "Lion") chasing a cut-out [bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear "Bear") was deemed inappropriate for children by parents for its unsettling tone, cinematography, and music. It was subsequently banned in several countries. A revised version of the sketch was aired several years later with adjusted editing and voice acting.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-94)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-95)

Although the programme is aimed at children between the ages of one and four, it had a substantial [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_following "Cult following") with older generations, mainly [university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University "University") and [college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College "College")[students](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student "Student").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Company2012-64)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Gutenko1998-96)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Brewer2010-97) The mixture of bright colours, unusual designs, repetitive non-verbal dialogue, ritualistic format, and occasional forays into physical comedy appealed to many who perceived the programme as having [psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_experience "Psychedelic experience") qualities.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-98) Shortly after the premiere of the show, at [Imperial College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_College_London "Imperial College London"), the campus activities calendar included airtimes and episode highlights.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Gutenko1998-96)

### Tinky Winky controversy

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/MardiGrasMarigny1999Falwell.JPG/250px-MardiGrasMarigny1999Falwell.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MardiGrasMarigny1999Falwell.JPG)

A group of people in Tinky Winky costumes at [Mardi Gras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mardi_Gras "Mardi Gras"), 1999

Controversy arose in 1999 concerning Tinky Winky's sexuality fuelled by him carrying a bag that looks much like a woman's [handbag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handbag "Handbag") (although he was first "[outed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outing "Outing")" by the academic and cultural critic Andy Medhurst in a letter from July 1997 to _[The Face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Face\_(magazine) "The Face (magazine)")_).[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-99) He aroused the interest of [Jerry Falwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Falwell "Jerry Falwell") in 1999 when Falwell alleged that the character was a "[gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay "Gay") role model". Falwell issued an attack in his _National Liberty Journal_, citing a _[Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington\_Post "Washington Post")_ "In/out" column which stated that [lesbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesbian "Lesbian") comedian [Ellen DeGeneres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_DeGeneres "Ellen DeGeneres") was "out" as the chief national gay representative, while trendy Tinky Winky was "in". He warned parents that Tinky Winky could be a covert homosexual symbol, because "he is [purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple "Purple"), the [gay pride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_pride "Gay pride") colour, and his antenna is shaped like a triangle: the [gay pride symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_triangle "Pink triangle")."[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-100) The BBC made an official response, explaining that "Tinky Winky is simply a sweet, technological baby with a magic bag."[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-Kraidy2007-101) Kenn Viselman of Itsy-Bitsy Entertainment commented, "He's not gay. He's not [straight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterosexuality "Heterosexuality"). He's just a character in a children's series."[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-102)

In May 2007, [Polish Ombudsman for Children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_ombudsman#Poland "Children's ombudsman")[Ewa Sowińska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ewa_Sowi%C5%84ska "Ewa Sowińska") revisited the matter, and planned to order an investigation.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-103) "I noticed that he has a woman's handbag, but I didn't realise he's a boy", Sowińska said in a public statement. She asked her office's [psychologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychologist "Psychologist") to look into the allegations. After the research in late 2007, she stated: "The opinion of a leading [sexologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexologist "Sexologist"), who maintains that this series has no negative effects on a child's psychology, is perfectly credible. As a result, I have decided that it is no longer necessary to seek the opinion of other psychologists."[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-104)

Despite the objections, the _[Independent on Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent\_on\_Sunday "Independent on Sunday")_'s editors included Tinky Winky as the only fictional character in the 2008 inaugural "[Happy List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_List "Happy List")", alongside 99 real-life adults recognised for making Britain a better and happier place.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-list2009-105)

In response to this controversy, the gay community embraced the Teletubbies, with Tinky Winky leading pride parades[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-106) and being featured on restaurant menus with themed items.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-107) In 2021, WildBrain, owner of the Teletubbies brand, declared their support for the LGBTQ+ community with the statement "Teletubbies Love Pride." The company released a limited collection of merchandise with proceeds supporting [GLAAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLAAD "GLAAD"). In a statement, WildBrain said, "The Teletubbies have always embraced their own offbeat quirkiness and sense of style. This Pride Month, we're celebrating that 'love who you are' spirit through our Collection of ready-to-rave fashion that makes Tinky Winky, Dipsy, Laa-Laa and Po very proud."[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-108)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-109) This was followed up by a 30-piece gender-fluid adult fashion collection commemorating Pride 2022.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletubbies#cite_note-110)
